bib.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know", Saurav Kadavath, Tom Conerly, Amanda Askell, ... Jared Kaplan (Anthropic). Preprint: the text reads "arXiv:2207.05221v4 [cs.CL] 21 Nov 2022". The PDF names no venue. v1 is 2022.

COVERAGE: I read all 114,288 of 114,288 chars (43 pages), covering the body, Sections 1–7, Appendices A–D, the Table 4 dataset list and the reference list. I filtered out lines that were only plot-axis numbers. The references I skimmed. pypdf hit a form-XObject limit warning, but all text seems to be there (see PROBLEMS). Only Table 1 (P(IK)) and Tables 2–3 contain exact numbers. Every multiple-choice and P(True) calibration result appears only as a plot, so the text gives no exact ECE values.

CLAIMS
- claim: Pretrained models only. Sizes 800M, 3B, 12B and 52B, pretrained on 850B tokens with about 10% code. RLHF policies appear only in Section 3.3.
  number: 800M/3B/12B/52B; 850B tokens
  setup: architecture as Bai et al. 2022
  quote: "We study a series of language models with 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B parameters. ... pretrained for 850B tokens, rather than the 400B tokens used in that work. ... In section 3.3 we brieﬂy study helpful and harmless RLHF policies ... but otherwise we only study pure language models."
  where: p.6, char ~17722
- claim: (a) Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice when the options are visible and labelled with letters. Calibration improves with size and from 0-shot to few-shot. The good calibration already holds 0-shot. The BIG Bench default format (rewriting the full answer) is calibrated less well.
  number: 5-shot vs 0-shot (Fig 4/5). The text gives no ECE values.
  setup: all BIG Bench MC tasks, MMLU, TruthfulQA, QuALITY, LogiQA
  quote: "We typically ﬁnd good calibration 0-shot, without any other prompt, though calibration improves as we pass from 0-shot to few-shot. We ﬁnd that in almost all cases, calibration improves with model size and capability." / "It is crucial that the model gets to see the answer choices explicitly before choosing amongst them" / "We ﬁnd that calibration is poorer in this format, compared to a format with lettered choices" (App A.4)
  where: p.8, char ~25193; p.25
- claim: Replacing the last option with "none of the above" hurts both accuracy and calibration significantly. Even the 52B model avoids that option, and 20-shot does not help.
  number: 5-shot, 20-shot
  setup: MMLU / BIG Bench
  quote: "even the 52B model is biased against using the “none of the above” option ... This is particularly surprising for 5-shot evaluations; we also tried evaluating 20-shot and this also did not improve performance."
  where: p.10, char ~30067
- claim: In a True/False reformulation of the MC tasks with human-written options, the 52B model is well calibrated, except that it is overconfident near the tails.
  number: 52B, 5-shot
  quote: "The 52B model is very well-calibrated except near the tails, where it is overconﬁdent."
  where: p.10, char ~29426
- claim: (c) Taken at face value, RLHF policies look very miscalibrated. A single temperature of T = 2.5 largely fixes this on three evaluations. The authors call it a "quick experiment" and note that heavier RL might not be fixable this way.
  number: T = 2.5
  setup: 52B HH RLHF policy, 5-shot, on MMLU, MMLU True/False and TruthfulQA (Fig 9)
  quote: "these policies naively appear very miscalibrated ... a simple temperature adjustment (with the same temperature T = 2 .5 for all evaluations) largely ﬁxes calibration issues with several independent evaluation tasks" / "Of course more intensive RL training might distort calibration in ways that cannot be remedied in this way"
  where: p.11, char ~32055–32704
- claim: (b) P(True) self-evaluation of the model's own T=1 samples is poorly calibrated zero-shot and sits near 50%. The cause given is that own samples lie near the decision boundary or the model is overconfident in them.
  number: 50%
  setup: TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex HumanEval
  quote: "These samples may lie close to the model’s own decision boundary for validity (or the model may simply be overconﬁdent about its own samples) ... Zero-shot, P(True) is poorly calibrated, and typically it lies close to 50% for typical samples (see Figure 38 in the appendix for illustrations)."
  where: p.12, char ~36947
- claim: AUDIT CAVEAT. "Zero-shot" in this paper still includes a fixed human-written prompt with six examples (App A.5). In the zero-shot runs the 52B separates correct from incorrect samples well, but the probability is not calibrated. On arithmetic, almost all samples get P(True) > 0.5, which does not fit a blanket "close to 50%".
  number: six examples; > 0.5
  quote: "P(True) provides very noticeable separation between correct and incorrect samples with the 52B model, but the probability itself is not calibrated. In particular, almost all samples from arithmetic questions have P(True)> 0.5. These evaluations are all zero-shot, but they include a human-written prompt with six examples."
  where: p.40 (Fig 38), char ~101387
- claim: Few-shot (20-shot) P(True) is well calibrated. A larger k mainly improves calibration, not AUROC. Zero-shot calibration improves with size but stays poor.
  number: 20-shot
  quote: "Self-evaluations are well-calibrated few-shot, though models aren’t as well-calibrated zero-shot. In particular, larger k for k-shot self-evaluation seems to primarily help by improving calibration, rather than by improving the AUROC" / Fig 34: "the P(True) judgment is poorly calibrated, though in most cases it seems to be improving as models become larger and more capable."
  where: p.4, char ~11432; p.38
- claim: Caveat on the 20-shot calibration plots. Small models look calibrated on GSM8k, Codex and Arithmetic only because they get almost everything wrong.
  number: none
  quote: "smaller models get almost every question wrong, which means that in these cases the small models are only well-calibrated because they are making trivial predictions."
  where: p.36 (Fig 32)
- claim: Showing five T=1 samples ("brainstormed ideas") improves self-evaluation significantly on short-form tasks and less on long-form ones (Codex, GSM8k). By Brier score, 20-shot with comparison samples is best in every case. By conditional accuracy, the fixed prompt beats 20-shot on Codex and GSM8k.
  number: 5 samples; 20-shot
  quote: "performance improves signiﬁcantly on all of the short-form answer tasks ... models beneﬁt less from this approach on tasks requiring long-form answers (Codex and GMS8k)" / "20-shot evaluation with comparison samples performs best in every case" / "it appears that the prompt actually performs better than few-shot for codex and GSM8k, possibly because these have long-form answers."
  where: p.12–13, char ~40342; p.33, char ~92103
- claim: For the 52B, answers with P(True) > 0.5 are far more often correct than the base rate, and the gap grows with size ("verification is often easier than generation"). The text gives no exact accuracies.
  number: P(True) > 50%
  quote: "for our 52B models answers labeled with P(True) > 50% are far more likely to be correct as compared to generic responses"
  where: p.11, char ~33819
- claim: (d) A P(IK) value head fine-tuned only on TriviaQA generalises partially out of distribution. Calibration on the new tasks is poor, mostly underconfident, and on Lambada it is "terrible". Training on all four tasks closes much of the gap.
  number: Table 1, 52B, AUROC / Brier (TriviaQA-only → all except GSM8K): TriviaQA 0.864/0.151 → 0.873/0.145; Mixed-Arithmetic 0.928/0.194 → 0.987/0.042; LAMBADA 0.606/0.431 → 0.853/0.108; Python Func Synth 0.687/0.164 → 0.881/0.109; GSM8K 0.624/0.200 → 0.752/0.121
  setup: 30 samples at T=1 per question give a soft label. The whole model is fine-tuned with the head.
  quote: "TriviaQA 0.864 / 0.151 0.873 / 0.145 / Mixed-Arithmetic 0.928 / 0.194 0.987 / 0.042 / LAMBADA 0.606 / 0.431 0.853 / 0.108 / Python Func Synth. 0.687 / 0.164 0.881 / 0.109 / GSM8K 0.624 / 0.200 0.752 / 0.121" / "OOD calibration of P(IK) is often quite poor, and for the most part models are underconﬁdent." / "when testing on Lambada, calibration was terrible, because the model produces uniformly low P(IK) scores"
  where: p.18, char ~52148; p.15, char ~46986, ~48093
- claim: P(IK) rises when relevant source material is in the context. Example: 18% becomes 78% when a Wikipedia article is added. The rise is larger for shorter articles. P(IK) also rises with GSM8k hints, more for good hints than bad ones, and falls for irrelevant hints.
  number: 18% → 78%
  quote: "P(IK) appropriately predicts a low value, speciﬁcally 18% for a 52B model" / "then the P(IK) score rises to 78%"
  where: p.18–19, char ~53517, ~55085
- claim: P(IK) carries only a weak model-specific signal. Two 12B models with different pretraining data differ by about 6%.
  number: 0.463 vs 0.408; ~6%
  quote: "the difference in P(IK) is only around 6%, so there is room for improvement from future work."
  where: p.21, char ~61192
- claim: Entropy of the answer distribution, H(A|Q), is not a robust "knows it" signal. Its AUROC on HumanEval falls with model size because larger models give diverse correct answers.
  number: N = 200 samples
  quote: "we believe that H(A|Q) is not a robust measure of whether or not a model knows the answer to a question, especially as models increase in size."
  where: App B.2, p.29

LIMITS: The authors' own text says: "models that have been ﬁnetuned for a speciﬁc purpose, such as RLHF policies [Bai et al., 2022], will not be so well-calibrated, and some of the methods we discussed may not work as well" (p.23, char ~67290). They also say they "only studied ﬁve sampling-based datasets", that the findings are "limited in power and scope", that they do not separate "the truth" from "what humans say", and that they do not address deception. They report that the natural-language P(IK) variant showed no major gains. Dated aspects: the work uses 2022 Anthropic base models up to 52B and only one RLHF temperature experiment. A model also cannot tell its own tokens from tokens it was given (footnote 1).

Audit notes:
(1) Note 05 is accurate on 50% / 20-shot / long-form. It should add that "zero-shot" here means a 6-example fixed prompt, and that arithmetic is an exception where P(True) > 0.5 for nearly all samples.
(2) The line in the 01 note ("P(True) ... well calibrated for large models in the right format") merges two results. "Right format" is the paper's claim about multiple choice and True/False on human-written options. For P(True) on the model's own samples, good calibration needs few-shot.
(3) The note 05 sentence "RLHF-tuned models are less well calibrated" is supported, but the paper also shows that T = 2.5 largely fixes it.

BUILDS ON: Guo et al., 2017 (token calibration); Srivastava et al., 2022 (BIG Bench, calibration improves with size); Rae et al., 2021 (Gopher MMLU calibration, which inspired the lettered format); Bai et al., 2022 (models/RLHF); Lin et al., 2022 (verbalised uncertainty, a P(True) analogue); Mielke et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022 (self-consistency); Desai and Durrett, 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Askell et al., 2021 (honesty).

CODE: The P(True) self-evaluation prompt (p.11, char ~36000):
```
Question: Who was the first president of the United States?
Proposed Answer: George Washington was the first president.
Is the proposed answer:
(A) True
(B) False
The proposed answer is:
```
The comparison-sample variant (p.12) inserts "Here are some brainstormed ideas: <5 T=1 samples>" and "Possible Answer:".

FIGURES:
- Fig 1, p.3: P(True) histograms for the 52B at 20-shot, plus the gain in accuracy from P(True) > 0.5. A one-glance summary.
- Fig 4, p.7: ECE against size for lettered 0-shot/5-shot, True/False and the BB default format. Shows the format and shot effects together.
- Fig 9, p.11: RLHF at T=1 against T=2.5. The temperature fix is visible immediately.
- Fig 11, p.13: Brier score and conditional accuracy for Lambada against Codex. Shows short-form versus long-form.
- Fig 38, p.40: Zero-shot P(True) histograms showing separation without calibration.
- Fig 13/16, p.15/17: P(IK) calibration in-distribution against OOD.
